title: In 22 larval zebrafish, brain regions with more projectome input did not have longer neuron activity timescales; a weak negative trend followed the lower signal fraction of those regions
abstract: Question: in primate models and human fMRI, brain regions with more structural input have longer intrinsic activity timescales. We tested this rule in the whole larval zebrafish brain. Data: Legare et al. 2025 two-photon calcium imaging (22 fish, 52,000-79,000 neurons each, about 1 Hz, 630 s of spontaneous activity) and the mapZebrain-derived directed region matrix from the same data set. Method (pre-specified): for each neuron we fitted an exponential decay to the autocorrelation at lags 1-30 s. For each region we took the fish-centred median log timescale. We correlated it with the region input strength across 58 regions, with a spatial-autocorrelation null and partial correlations for position, neuron count, signal fraction and imaging plane. Results: the prediction failed. The relation was negative and not significant (Spearman rho -0.25, 95% CI -0.47 to 0.00, spatial p 0.16, partial rho -0.22, p 0.12). The timescale map was reliable across fish (split-half rho 0.90), but input strength did not explain it. High-input regions had a lower calcium signal fraction (rho -0.59). With only high-signal neurons (rho 0.00) or with signal-adjusted timescales (rho 0.00), no trend remained. Region-average signals gave rho -0.04. Removal of global or principal-component activity did not give a positive relation. Together with earlier campaign results for mouse cortex and C. elegans, none of five data sets in three animals showed the positive input-timescale relation. Limitations: nuclear GCaMP6s at 1 Hz resolves only multi-second timescales; most neurons have a small signal fraction; the structural matrix is an atlas average from a limited set of reconstructed neurons; 58 regions give limited power for rho below about 0.35.
